rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding discussion of Qur’an deniers and the Prophet’s rejection, people are addressed directly and the Qur’an’s qualities are explained as a divine treasure they fail to value.
rows.anchor: Now these people are addressed directly and the nature of the treasure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As counsel, the Qur’an warns people of dangers and scolds those blindly advancing toward them.
rows.anchor: it informs people of the dangers they need to protect themselves from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an cures diseases of the heart that strip people of human traits and, as punishment, disable them from accepting guidance, making them worse than animals.
rows.anchor: These ailments divest people of all human traits and as punishment they lose the ability to accept guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an treats the heart as the fountainhead of wisdom and insight and the center of real life, determination, and action; people are alive only when their hearts are alive.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān regards the heart to be the fountainhead of all wisdom and insight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance and mercy encompass the Qur’an’s worldly and otherworldly roles: it guides people here and guarantees mercy in the Hereafter to those who accept it.
rows.anchor: this Book is guidance in this world for people and those who accept it, it is a guarantee of mercy in the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted verb is understood to say that the Qur’an has brought God’s grace and mercy; people should embrace this lasting treasure instead of worldly acquisitions.
rows.anchor: this Qur’ān has brought the grace and mercy of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding direct address about the Qur’an, the discourse returns to monotheism and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Now once again monotheism and the hereafter are mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arab idolaters claimed their self-invented halal and haram regulations came from God; this imputes falsehood to Him and is a heinous sin.
rows.anchor: they claimed that it was God’s directive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unanswered question about the reckoning of those who falsely attribute laws to God expresses extreme gravity and anger, and implies they will face punishment at Judgment.
rows.anchor: The question is not even answered. This signifies the extreme anger of the speaker.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s graciousness gives wrongdoers respite and sustenance so they can reform and repent, though most respond with ingratitude and intensify their foolishness.
rows.anchor: such is His graciousness that He gives respite to people in spite of these great wrongdoings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance and glad tidings address the Prophet and his companions, who should not be troubled by their adversaries’ mischief.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) and his companions are addressed here and given assurance and glad tidings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about reciting from it, the pronoun refers to God’s Book mentioned in 10:57–58, and Qur’an here means a portion of that Book.
rows.anchor: the antecedent of the genetive pronoun is the Book of God referred to earlier in verses 57-58

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural address includes the Prophet’s companions, so the assurance and glad tidings are not limited to him; they too endangered their lives for God’s religion.
rows.anchor: this assurance and these glad tidings are not specific to him. His companions are also included.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb with this preposition means being engrossed; it depicts the companions’ intense devotion and heightens the assurance that God watches over and protects the Prophet.
rows.anchor: is used with the preposition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will answer the enemies’ questions at the proper time, while the Prophet and his companions should remain patient.
rows.anchor: As for the Prophet (sws) and his companions, they should be patient.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hud 11:12 passage exemplifies the disbelievers’ sarcastic remarks that could be directed at the Prophet.
rows.anchor: One such example can be seen in verse 12 of Sūrah Hūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unnamed expression ‘Listen: for the friends of God’ identifies the preceding group; their Hereafter has neither regret over the past nor fear of the future.
rows.anchor: the one of God’s friends and for them are glad tidings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith and fearing God are the qualities that make someone eligible for divine friendship and its promised consequence.
rows.anchor: are for those who have them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice makes His messengers and their companions prevail over adversaries in this world, though this does not apply to prophets who were not messengers.
rows.anchor: they and their companions are destined to prevail over their adversaries in this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘God’s words can never change’ means His promises will certainly be fulfilled; the believers’ promised outcome is real and great success.
rows.anchor: refers to the promises of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ comments are sarcastic and biting; their ridicule could target the prophecy of Muslim dominance despite the Muslims’ poverty and unmet basic needs.
rows.anchor: The expression “What they say should not grieve you” refer to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is assured that the prophecy will materialize because God, master of honor, can confer honor on him and his companions beyond anyone’s power to prevent.
rows.anchor: God is the master of honour and respect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing attributes teach the Prophet and companions patience and trust; God hears and knows their enemies’ unspoken questions and will answer them in due time.
rows.anchor: The attributes mentioned in the end are meant to instruct

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following verses addressed to the Prophet, the passage resumes its discussion of monotheism.
rows.anchor: The previous verses, as indicated, addressed the Prophet (sws). The topic of monotheism that was under discussion is now once again taken up.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for conjecture denotes a wholly speculative opinion unsupported by sound knowledge, intellect, or intuition.
rows.anchor: It is something totally speculative.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic linguistic principles permit parallel portions of the verse to be suppressed; the author supplies an expanded wording to make them explicit.
rows.anchor: parallel portions have been suppressed keeping in view linguistic principles of Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the signs in verse 67 are not specified there, other Qur’anic passages explain them.
rows.anchor: I will refer to some of them here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The complementary night and day serve human needs, while the harmony of opposites points to a sovereign, wise will coordinating the universe and proves monotheism.
rows.anchor: Together both are serving the needs of human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe is not accidental or an entertainer’s playfield; its every part displays great power, amazing wisdom, and deep purpose.
rows.anchor: this universe has not come into being as a result of an accident nor is it the playfield of an entertainer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word used for the alleged child applies to singular and plural, masculine and feminine entities; reading it as ‘son’ is linguistically wrong and conflicts with Arab belief, which identified angels as God’s daughters.
rows.anchor: Those who regard it to means a son have faltered. This meaning is against linguistic usage as well as the beliefs of the Arabs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assigning children to God is incompatible with His attributes because it would make them parts or peers of His being and compromise His peerlessness.
rows.anchor: it is against God’s attributes to assign children to Him because children would be a part of His being and His peers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s self-sufficiency rules out children: humans need them for procreation, help, and support in old age, but God needs nothing and owns all creation.
rows.anchor: God is beyond all these needs and whatever is in the heavens and the earth belong to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section VI gives detailed accounts of Noah and Moses and brief accounts of intervening messengers to repeat earlier arguments from human nature and reason, reassure the Prophet and companions, and warn their adversaries; the underlying story remains the same across times and places.
rows.anchor: The purpose of these historical tales is to highlight the same things that have been highlighted earlier through arguments drawn from human nature and intellect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe’s purposeful design means it should neither continue purposelessly nor end abruptly; it must culminate in an objective achievable only through belief in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: it is essential that it culminate on a great objective and this objective cannot be achieved unless the Hereafter is acknowledged.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pervasive providential system entails accountability: people owe their sustainer an obligation, so those who recognize it merit reward and those who disregard it deserve punishment.
rows.anchor: Providence entails accountability.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s people were the oldest destroyed nation whose story was well known to Arabs, explaining why the Qur’an places them first in chronological accounts; al-A‘rāf gives their region and approximate era.
rows.anchor: it is this nation which is mentioned the foremost.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term naba denotes an important event, marking a decisive historical moment rather than mere historical narration.
rows.anchor: means some important event. Thus it is evident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s ‘stay’ means his prolonged preaching until opponents wearied of it, as also indicated in al-‘Ankabūt and Hūd; this remark precedes his challenge.
rows.anchor: he preached for a very long time until his adversaries got sick and tired of his preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words for opinion and decision and for something covering are explained lexically; idiomatically, the latter means hesitation or bewilderment. The preposition after the verb of deciding adds the sense of taking action, so Noah challenges them to execute their scheme without delay, trusting God as protector.
rows.anchor: Noah (sws) told them to go ahead and fulfil their scheme without giving him any respite for he trusted God as his protector.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah is untroubled if they persist in rejecting him: he seeks no payment and is not charged with forcing them to believe.
rows.anchor: He is not charging them for his preaching so that he may fear any loss.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account names Noah and his companions’ deliverance before the rejecters’ drowning because God’s established practice is to secure believers first when punishment comes.
rows.anchor: when the torment visits the rejecters, the believers are first secured by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to observe the warned nation’s fate points to the passage’s purpose: Quraysh likewise face destruction if they reject the Prophet after truth is conclusively conveyed.
rows.anchor: a similar fate awaits the Quraysh if they do not pay heed to the Prophet’s calls.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 74 briefly alludes to messengers sent after Noah; the succeeding sūrah Hūd, this sūrah’s counterpart, supplies fuller accounts.
rows.anchor: This concise and brief mention has been complemented with details in the succeeding sūrah: Hūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd expands the brief mention with accounts of Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shu‘ayb and additional details about Noah’s and Moses’s peoples; the Qur’an often first summarizes and later elaborates.
rows.anchor: This style of detailing out things after first mentioning them briefly is very commonly used in the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice is that those who deny truths evident to human nature and reason gain no benefit from messenger warnings; after conclusive communication, refusal seals their hearts. Exceeding God’s limits deadens the sense of obedience, leaving them unreachable by admonition.
rows.anchor: those who deny what is obvious from human nature and intellect receive no benefit from the warnings of the messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs Moses recited to Pharaoh and his courtiers include God’s revelations as well as the signs he displayed.
rows.anchor: the revelations of God which Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Pharaoh’s party wrongdoers refers to their corrupted hearts, minds, and intellects; as God’s messengers, Moses and Aaron had to convey the truth conclusively. The author rejects the view that Moses only sought Israelite national liberation without inviting Pharaoh to faith.
rows.anchor: Thus the view of those who believe that Moses (sws), like a nationalist leader, had only demanded the freedom of the Israelites from the Pharaoh and did not invite him to faith and religion is not correct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Truth’ means the manifest claim, supported by miracles, that Moses and Aaron are God’s messengers; Pharaoh’s party denied it, called the miracles magic, and claimed their own magicians had greater power.
rows.anchor: a clear and evident truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of ‘say’ is suppressed and the lām has an explanatory force; Moses’s phrasing means they call a clear truth magic. The word ‘magic’ is left unstated out of revulsion at applying it to truth.
rows.anchor: The reason that the word “magic” is suppressed here is that the speaker dislikes it to so much in relation to the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘when it has come to you’ stresses that denying an immediately witnessed truth is like denying the midday sun, unlike debate over what has not been observed.
rows.anchor: when it is right before a person’s eyes, then disputing it is like denying the mid-day sun.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Logic alone does not distinguish magic from miracle; their manifestation, effects on mind and heart, and presenters’ character do. Magic is temporary and fails against truth, so Moses’s words challenge Pharaoh to test the magicians against his miracles.
rows.anchor: the difference between magic and miracle is not evident through logic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s accusation was a politically charged charge of rebellion: Egyptian rulers feared Israelite population growth and circulated a rumor that Moses sought power to rouse Coptic resistance; killing Israelite boys was intended to limit that growth.
rows.anchor: one purpose of the cruel scheme of killing the male offspring of the Israelites was to check their growth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his courtiers knew Moses was no magician and his signs were not magic, but fearing loss of leadership they evaded the truth by staging a contest with their country’s expert magicians.
rows.anchor: neither was Moses (sws) a magician nor what he was presenting magic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s invitation for the magicians to begin shows confidence in God’s promise; their defeat in their chosen arena amounts to his first victory.
rows.anchor: This was like his first victory in the match because the defeat of the magicians which followed was in the area of their own choice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers the earlier accusation by saying the magicians’ display, not his miracle, is magic; God will destroy it, as confirmed by the cited declaration that truth has arrived and falsehood vanished.
rows.anchor: Now, here in verse 81, Moses (sws) responds by saying that what they are presenting was magic and not what he has presented.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iṣlāḥ here means bringing something to its outcome or making it bear fruit, also as in 47:2–5; wrongdoers cannot make their efforts prevail against reformers who preach truth, and the righteous triumph after trial.
rows.anchor: the efforts of the wrongdoers never bear fruit against the reformers who preach the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word dhurriyya conveys more than scarcity: at first only a few young people professed faith, despite their fear of Pharaoh and the nation’s elders.
rows.anchor: it also shows that initially only a few people from among the young professed faith in
